# The Name {#sec-the-name}

For about a month, the little program I had written to check my notes was called check.py.
That was what it did, and I was the only one who ever had to say it.

Then it was notes-check, which was more accurate and no better.

Then it was a folder with four files in it.
The notes had been a shoebox, then a spreadsheet, then a program, and each had grown too big for the one before.
This was the first of them that needed a name.

It needed one because it was about to become a repository: a place that keeps every version of a program, so you can always go back to an earlier one.
I made every change to the program at night, and some of them I could not undo in the morning.
I had been meaning to give it that kind of home for about a month.

You can name a folder anything.
You can't call a repository "the thing for chapter four".

So I set aside an evening for names.
I opened a blank document, and by midnight the list filled a whole page.

Most of them were puns, names that played on two meanings at once.
Punctuation makes puns easy, and it shouldn't.
One had the word *colon* in it, and I had not thought it through.

None of them was a name.
They were jokes I would have to explain every time I typed one.

I kept going, which is how two in the morning happens.

Around two I gave up on the page and opened a chat with Otto, meaning to ask something else entirely.
I typed "quirk".

Otto finished it as "quirework".

I looked at the word for a while.
It was not a pun.
It sounded like something that should already exist, and as far as I could find, it didn't.
I checked.

I liked it better than anything on the page.
I liked it better than anything I would have chosen, and I had spent the evening choosing.

I don't remember what I meant to ask.

I made the repository that night, before I could think better of it.
Every time you save a change to a repository, you write a short note saying what you did.
My first note said *Name it*.

I have written better notes since.
Not many.

In the morning I gave it a README, the page that tells a stranger what a tool is for and how to use it, because a repository without one looks abandoned.
I gave it a version number too, because a tool without one looks like a little program somebody wrote on a Sunday.
The version number was zero point one, which promises nothing.
The README was a page long.
It was the shortest it would ever be.

Chapter four had not changed in weeks.
It had never been so consistent.

That week the program stopped being a little program.
It had a name, a repository, a README and a version number.
It was a tool.

I was the only person who had ever used it.
